source.title: An Adaptive and Momental Bound Method for Stochastic Learning
source.authors: Jianbang Ding; Xuancheng Ren; Ruixuan Luo; Xu Sun

record.file_problem: not stated; the supplied text appears complete.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own training-accuracy results for CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 models trained with adaptive optimizers and SGDM, bearing on whether gradient training fits V1. It does not report the exact training-error values needed to establish near-zero error.
record.gate_note: Training-accuracy curves for the CIFAR models are figure-only. The text says AdaMod achieves better training performance than Adam and reaches its best training accuracy after learning-rate decay, but it does not give the plotted values. Cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The SGDM and Adam comparators measure training classification accuracy on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, matching V1's method and measure. Their plotted endpoints are unavailable in the supplied text, so near-zero training error cannot be established. AdaMod's comparative performance does not itself test V1's specified SGD/Adam result.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate: the authors attribute early training instability to extreme adaptive learning rates and report that AdaMod's moving-average upper bounds stabilize training and improve performance, especially for DenseNet and Transformer. They also acknowledge weaker performance than SGDM on some models and a convergence-speed cost from larger beta3.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares AdaMod with Adam and SGDM on CIFAR classification; it does not test the claim's stated zero-training-error recipes or label-corruption conditions.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that AdaMod's training loss on Transformer-small varies with β3; CIFAR learning-rate and β3 sweeps are also described, but they report test accuracy or convergence speed rather than the claim's near-zero training-error outcome.

fits_no_version.finding: AdaMod matches or improves CIFAR training performance relative to Adam; the supplied text does not provide absolute training-accuracy endpoints.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Bounding Adam's adaptive learning rates can improve optimization performance on CIFAR convolutional networks.

fits_no_version.finding: For Transformer translation training, Adam without warmup stalls around loss 9.5, whereas warmup reduces loss below 3.5; AdaMod trains without warmup. No stability threshold or curvature is measured.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Warmup or adaptive learning-rate bounds can prevent optimization failure in Transformer translation training.

record.problems: The CIFAR training-accuracy outcomes are shown only in figures and are not numerically stated in the text; the study does not state initialization or report corrupted-label training results.

untested.parts: Corrupted or random labels, model-size comparisons, early stopping, and controlled comparisons of regularization recipes are not tested. Initialization is unspecified.
No two-layer ReLU teacher-student experiment or measurement of spurious minima versus excess student width.
No controlled depth or identity-shortcut comparison, very deep plain tanh experiment, or Fixup experiment.
No comparison of initialization schemes, signal propagation, or trainable depth.
No initial linearized stability threshold, curvature trajectory, squared-loss catapult experiment, or full-batch edge-of-stability measurement.
No normalization ablation or Fixup comparison.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict label is justified because the V1-linked training-accuracy endpoints cannot be read from the supplied text. This is an evidence-access limitation, not a demonstrated failure of V1. Figure 8 reports AdaMod training accuracy under beta3 variation, but that method comparison does not supply a missing result for any stated version.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not state initialization, corrupted or random-label conditions, smaller-model or early-stopping comparisons, or whether training classification error reaches zero or near zero.
